implementation_notes: Akka supplies both halves of the pattern: the request-reply protocol (the recipient of responses is encoded as a replyTo: ActorRef[Response] field in the message, so no reply address is configured out of band) and the method-call shape (context.ask(responder, Message.apply) for a 1:1 request/response, failing with a TimeoutException when the response does not arrive within the implicit Timeout; outside an actor the AskPattern gives ref.ask[Reply](...): Future[Reply]). A gateway is then a thin trait whose methods wrap ask and map the response into domain types, so callers hold a plain reference instead of an ActorRef. When the sender should not accept the responder's response type at all, the documented alternative is a message adapter rather than asking.
pitfalls: ask has no retry and no delivery guarantee: on timeout it fails with TimeoutException while the request may still be processed remotely, so the timeout must mean 'unknown outcome' at the call site.
Asking from inside an actor as its normal protocol is discouraged - the response belongs in the actor's own protocol via a message adapter - so a facade that hides ask invites that misuse.
Every ask allocates a temporary actor to receive the response, so a facade fanning out to many services needs deliberate bounds on concurrent pending asks.
